title: Solar-Powered Water Purification System
prompt:
Design a standalone solar-powered reverse osmosis (RO) desalination system that fits inside a standard 20-foot shipping container (internal dimensions: 5.9 m × 2.35 m × 2.39 m) and produces 5,000 litres per day of potable water from seawater, with a total system cost under $50,000 USD.

Design conditions:
- Feed water: seawater at 35,000 ppm TDS (total dissolved solids), temperature 25°C.
- Product water: < 500 ppm TDS (WHO drinking water standard).
- Location: coastal site at latitude 25°N, average daily solar irradiance 5.5 kWh/m²/day on a tilted surface.
- Operating hours: 8 hours per day (peak solar hours with battery buffer for cloud transients).
- No grid connection. Fully off-grid.

Your design must include:

A. RO MEMBRANE SYSTEM:
1. Calculate the required feed pressure. The osmotic pressure of seawater at 35,000 ppm and 25°C is approximately 27 bar (use the van't Hoff equation: π = iMRT, with i ≈ 2 for NaCl, M ≈ 0.6 mol/L). The operating pressure must exceed osmotic pressure plus the osmotic pressure of the concentrate at the system recovery ratio.
2. State the recovery ratio (permeate/feed). For seawater RO, typical single-pass recovery is 35-45%. At higher recovery, osmotic pressure of the concentrate increases non-linearly. If you use 40% recovery, the concentrate TDS is 35000/(1-0.4) = 58,333 ppm with osmotic pressure ~45 bar.
3. Calculate the required feed flow rate: if producing 5000 L/day at R% recovery over 8 hours, feed flow = (5000/8)/(R/100) L/h.
4. Select an appropriate membrane element (e.g., 4-inch or 8-inch spiral-wound). State the membrane area per element, permeate flux, and number of elements needed. Standard seawater RO membranes operate at 12-18 LMH (litres per square metre per hour).
5. Determine whether staging is required (single stage vs. two-stage). For seawater at this recovery, a single stage with 6-7 elements in series per pressure vessel is typical.

B. ENERGY SYSTEM:
1. Calculate the specific energy consumption (SEC) of the RO system in kWh/m³. For seawater RO without energy recovery: SEC ≈ 4-6 kWh/m³. With an energy recovery device (pressure exchanger or turbocharger): SEC ≈ 2.5-3.5 kWh/m³.
2. State whether you use an energy recovery device and justify the choice (cost vs. energy saving).
3. Calculate total daily energy requirement: SEC × 5 m³/day.
4. Size the solar PV array: energy required / (irradiance × system losses). Use a system loss factor of 0.75-0.80 (accounting for inverter efficiency, wiring losses, temperature derating, soiling).
5. Calculate the required panel area and verify it fits on/around the container.
6. Size a battery bank for cloud buffering (minimum 2 hours of autonomy at full load).

C. COST ESTIMATE:
Itemize costs: solar panels, batteries, charge controller/inverter, RO membranes, high-pressure pump, energy recovery device (if used), pre-treatment (multimedia filter, cartridge filter), controls/instrumentation, container modification, plumbing and fittings. Verify total < $50,000.

D. CONSTRAINT VERIFICATION TABLE:
Present all constraints and achieved values: production rate, water quality, container fit (dimensions), cost, and energy self-sufficiency.
verification_method: Check: (1) Osmotic pressure calculation at the concentrate end is correct (not just the feed end — this is the most common error). At 40% recovery, concentrate is 58,333 ppm with π ≈ 45 bar, so operating pressure must be ≥ 55-60 bar. (2) Feed flow rate calculation is consistent with recovery and production. (3) Number of membrane elements is consistent with required permeate flow and membrane flux. (4) Energy calculation: SEC × daily production = daily energy need. PV sizing accounts for irradiance and losses. (5) Total panel area fits the container roof (~14 m²) or includes ground-mounted panels with justification. (6) Cost estimate is itemised and plausible (solar panels ~$0.30-0.50/W, SW RO membranes ~$500-800 each, high-pressure pump ~$3000-5000).
why_frontier_hard: Three coupled engineering domains (membrane separation, solar energy, system integration) with non-linear interactions. The primary failure mode is the osmotic pressure at high recovery: models frequently use the feed osmotic pressure (27 bar) as the required operating pressure, ignoring the concentrate end where osmotic pressure is much higher. The second failure mode is energy: without an energy recovery device, SEC is ~5 kWh/m³, requiring 25 kWh/day. At 5.5 kWh/m²/day with 0.77 system efficiency, that needs ~6 kW of panels (~18 m², exceeding the container roof area). This forces either an ERD (adding cost) or ground-mounted panels (adding complexity). Models typically get one domain right but not all three.
ground_truth_notes: At 40% recovery: feed flow = 5000/(8×0.4) = 1562.5 L/h. Concentrate osmotic pressure ≈ 45 bar. Operating pressure ≈ 55-60 bar. With 4-inch SW membranes at 15 LMH and 7.9 m² per element, each element produces ~120 L/h, needing ~5-6 elements for 625 L/h permeate. SEC without ERD: ~5 kWh/m³ = 25 kWh/day. With ERD: ~3 kWh/m³ = 15 kWh/day. PV sizing without ERD: 25/(5.5×0.77) ≈ 5.9 kW ≈ 18 m² of panels. Container roof is only ~14 m², so either ERD is needed or some panels are ground-mounted. Budget is tight at $50k — ERD costs ~$5-8k but saves ~$3k in PV.
